title: Control feedbunker and water trough quality

lessons.title: Reading and scoring the feed bunker
lessons.html:
Why bunk reading matters

In a feedlot, profit depends on cattle eating as much good feed as they can, every day, without waste and without digestive upsets. The bunk reader checks every bunker before feeding and decides whether each pen gets more, the same or less feed. Overfeeding wastes feed that goes stale; underfeeding slows growth and makes cattle hungry so they gorge at the next feed, which can cause acidosis and bloat.

When and how to read

Read bunkers at the same time each day, usually early morning before the first feed. Walk or drive slowly along each bunker and look at how much feed is left and what it looks like. Many feedlots use a simple scoring scale, for example:

ScoreWhat you seeUsual action
Clean, lickedNo feed, bunker polishedIncrease as per feedlot rule
SlickFew scattered particlesKeep the same or small increase
Some feedThin layer along the bunkerKeep the same
Lots of feedMuch feed leftDecrease and check the pen

Use the exact scale and the increase or decrease amounts set by your feedlot manager or nutritionist. Record the score for every pen on the bunk sheet.

Look at the cattle too

Read the pen as well as the bunker. Cattle waiting at the bunker and bellowing are hungry. Many cattle lying down and not coming to eat may be sick, overfed or stressed by heat or mud. Look for loose dung, bloated cattle, lame animals and any that stand alone. Report pulls to the animal health team immediately.

Ration changes

When cattle move from starter to grower to finisher rations, changes must be gradual according to the feedlot step-up program. Watch those pens even more closely in the days after a change.

lessons.title: Keeping feed bunkers clean and the feed fresh
lessons.html:
Bunker condition

A bunker is the cattle's plate. Dirty, wet or mouldy feed reduces intake and can make cattle ill.

What to check

  • Old feed – feed left for a long time heats up, goes sour and moulds, especially in hot or wet weather. Remove it before fresh feed is delivered.
  • Wet feed – after rain, feed in the bunker gets soggy. Clean it out and dry the bunker as far as possible.
  • Contamination – dung, birds, stones, wire, plastic and dead rodents must be removed.
  • Damage – cracked concrete, broken neck rails or sharp edges that can injure cattle.

Cleaning routine

  1. Follow the feedlot schedule, for example scraping bunkers out on set days and whenever the bunk reader marks them.
  2. Weigh or estimate the feed removed and record it, so the feed office knows the real intake.
  3. Dispose of removed feed where the manager instructs, never back into the mixer.
  4. Report damage for repair.

Bird and fly control

Large flocks of birds eat and foul feed and can spread disease. Flies breed in old wet feed and manure. Good bunker hygiene, removing spilt feed and keeping the area around bunkers dry are the first line of control. Any chemical control must use registered products according to the label under Act 36 of 1947, and only by trained staff.

Safety

Work along bunkers only when feed trucks and loaders are not moving there, and stay visible. Do not climb into pens with cattle unless you are trained and another person knows where you are.

lessons.title: Water trough quality and control
lessons.html:
Water is the most important nutrient

Cattle drink more on hot days and when they eat more dry feed. If water is short, dirty or hot, cattle eat less and grow slowly. A dirty trough can also spread disease between animals.

Daily checks

  • Is water flowing and is the float valve working? Is the trough full?
  • Is the water clean, without algae, feed, dung, dead birds or foam?
  • Is there a leak causing mud around the trough? Mud leads to lameness and flies.
  • Are cattle crowding the trough? There may be too little trough space or slow refill.

Cleaning troughs

  1. Clean on the schedule set by the feedlot, often several times a week in summer, and whenever a trough is dirty.
  2. Close the supply, drain the trough, scrub the sides and bottom with a hard brush and remove all slime.
  3. Use only cleaning products approved by your manager and rinse well so no chemical remains.
  4. Refill and check that the float closes properly.
  5. Record the date, pen and any problem found.

Water supply and quality

Report low pressure, broken pipes and changes in colour, taste or smell of the water. The manager may have the water tested for salts, nitrates or bacteria. Water use is also controlled under the National Water Act 36 of 1998, so leaks waste a resource the farm is responsible for.

Key points

  • Read bunkers at the same time every day and record a score for each pen.
  • Use the feedlot's scale and rules to adjust feed; never guess.
  • Remove old, wet or contaminated feed before fresh feed is given.
  • Check every water trough daily for flow, cleanliness and leaks.
  • Report sick cattle, damage and water problems at once.

quiz.question: When should bunkers usually be read?

options.text: Any time it suits the reader
At the same time each day, usually before the first feed

quiz.question: A bunker has a lot of feed left in the morning. What is the usual action?

options.text: Decrease the feed and check the pen

quiz.question: Why is underfeeding a pen a problem?

options.text: Hungry cattle gorge at the next feed, which can cause acidosis

quiz.question: What should be done with old, sour feed removed from a bunker?

options.text: Put it back in the mixer
Record it and dispose of it where the manager instructs

quiz.question: Mud around a water trough is a sign of what?

options.text: A leak that can lead to lameness and flies

quiz.question: Ration changes from starter to finisher should be made suddenly to save time.
After cleaning a trough with a chemical, it must be rinsed well before refilling.
Which should be checked at every water trough daily? (select all that apply)

options.text: Algae, dung or dead birds in the water
